title: Yahoo Bounces Back via the Internet OG: Self-Developed AI Q&A Engine Scout Targets Gen Z
excerpt: Yahoo CEO Jim Lanzone said that as an "elder" of the Internet born in 1994, Yahoo's brand awareness has become a unique advantage in the current context of decl
content_html:
Yahoo CEO Jim Lanzone said that as an "elder" of the Internet born in 1994, Yahoo's brand awareness has become a unique advantage in the current context of declining trust, and the company is attracting the Z generation with this vintage label, while seeking growth through self-developed AI tools. Since joining Yahoo in 2021, Lanzone has been working to reshape the internet pioneer, which was acquired by Apollo, into a more streamlined consumer technology group.

Scout Answer Engine and Differentiated Data Cards

This transformation comes as Yahoo tries to prove its place in the AI era, despite years of being in the shadow of giants like Google. The company plans to fully launch its AI-driven "answer engine" Scout later this year, along with several editorial and consumer products; Scout will integrate open web information with Yahoo's own content archives, user data, and 30 years of search history, with the technology licensed from multiple AI companies.

Lanzone believes that Yahoo's decades of accumulated proprietary search, content, and user data can make its AI products different from competitors that are mainly trained on open web data, so the company has chosen not to license content to other tech groups for model training. In terms of commercialization, Yahoo plans to use advertising to fund its AI answer service, allowing search ads to follow users into the AI answer space; in addition to Scout, it has also launched an investment platform for retail investors called AlphaSpace and continues to expand its subscription products. Wall Street expects Yahoo to go public or seek a sale as early as next year, but Lanzone did not comment, only emphasizing that "becoming a growth company first" is the current focus.
